newsitem.title: UK: Scientists count all the genes in ulcer bug.
newsitem.headline: Scientists count all the genes in ulcer bug.

text.p: U.S. researchers said on Wednesday they had counted and identified every single gene in a microbe that causes stomach ulcers and cancer.

Craig Venter and his team at The Institute for Genomic Research (TIGR) in Rockville, Maryland said they had completely sequenced the genome of Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium that commonly infects the stomach.
"This is information that I think scientists are going to use for centuries," Venter said in a telephone interview.
"They are fundamental discoveries about the basic essence of nature and as such will probably have an impact for a very, very long time."
It is only recently that scientists have realised that stomach ulcers and, eventually, cancer, could be caused by a bacterial infection.
H pylori is also responsible for most ulcers of the duodenum, the very first part of the intestine which attaches to the stomach.
Since H pylori has been identified as the villain, doctors have reported cures for stomach ulcers using antibiotics. But it usually takes a long time and several antibiotics are often required.
Sequencing the genome -- identifying every single gene -- can help scientists target vulnerable parts of the bacterium and design more effective drugs to eradicate it.
H pylori is only the fifth bacterium to have been entirely sequenced, and the fourth to be done by TIGR, which was set up specifically to do such work.
More than half the world's population may be infected with H pylori, which researchers believe can be passed on by personal contact. Crowded living conditions are one big risk factor.

The bacterium has 1,590 genes arranged on a single, circular chromosome, the TIGR team reported in a paper published in the science journal Nature. Humans have 80,000 genes on 46 x-shaped chromosomes.
Analysis of the bacterium's genes shows it is similar to other bacteria such as its cousin E coli and probably eats glucose, as well as amino acids.
"We have a unique perspective," Venter said. "We are seeing these for the first time in history from in the inside out."
Venter's 150 scientists were working on the bacteria responsible for tuberculosis and cholera. "By the end of next year we should have up to a dozen more," he said.
"Is this new sequence big news?" Russell Doolittle, a molecular geneticist at the University of California at San Diego, asked in a commentary in Nature.
"The answer has to be a resounding 'yes' -- Helicobacter pylori is the organism that causes peptic ulcers and, astonishingly, it may infect as much as half the world's population."
Drug companies have paid millions for just small bits of genetic information about microbes, but TIGR is publishing all the information free on the World Wide Web.

"You might argue that I'm not very bright," Venter said. "If you're a business person I get the stupid award. But my view is that scientists around the world are going to use this information to make basic discoveries to move forward drug development and vaccine development more than any single company could do."
